title: AI-enhanced adaptive virtual screening of large libraries for ligand discovery - Nature Biotechnology
gist: AdaptiveFlow is an open-source ultralarge virtual screening platform that ships the 69-billion-compound Enamine REAL Space in ready-to-dock form and uses an 18-dimensional molecular-property grid to prescreen only ~12 million representative molecules, cutting screening cost up to 1,000-fold versus brute force while scaling near-linearly to 5.6 million AWS vCPUs. It delivered nanomolar inhibitors of FSP1 and a PARP1 inhibitor with an 8.8 nM IC50 comparable to olaparib, both confirmed by co-crystal structures.

insights.claim: Purchasable on-demand chemical space grew from roughly 2 billion molecules in 2020 to trillions today, which makes exhaustive docking economically obsolete rather than merely expensive.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Compute cost per screen is no longer the binding constraint on hit discovery — search strategy is; vendors selling raw docking throughput face commoditization.
insights.quote: The financial cost alone is a major bottleneck8, rendering it impractical as chemical databases continue to grow exponentially, with newer libraries exceeding 1 trillion compounds and growing.

insights.claim: Focusing screens on target-specific chemical subspaces is framed as a structural necessity rather than an optimization, because library growth is outrunning any plausible growth in compute budgets.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The winning platforms in computational drug discovery will be selection-algorithm companies, not compute-scale companies — a directional call on where value accrues.
insights.quote: As the chemical space continues to expand, focusing on target-specific subspaces will no longer be optional, but essential.

insights.claim: Traditional high-throughput screening samples only hundreds of thousands of compounds against an estimated 10^60 synthetically accessible drug-like molecules, a sampling gap that is most damaging for shallow or allosteric pockets and protein-protein interfaces.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The case for virtual screening is strongest precisely on the 'undruggable' targets where physical HTS libraries have historically failed — that is where computational platforms should be underwritten.
insights.quote: This minuscule sampling poses a major bottleneck, particularly for challenging targets such as protein–protein interaction interfaces or allosteric sites, where binding pockets are often shallow, dynamic or poorly defined.

insights.claim: The core method partitions a library into an 18-dimensional grid of physicochemical properties, docks one to ten representative molecules per occupied tranche as a prescreen, then fully screens only the top-scoring tranches.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A simple, transferable heuristic — property-space binning as a cheap proxy for binding potential — that competitors can replicate without proprietary ML.

insights.claim: Because the 69-billion-compound library occupies only about 12 million tranches averaging 5,600 molecules each, a single-representative prescreen requires just 12 million dockings — over 5,000-fold less computation than screening the full library.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Quantifies the cost collapse: a billion-scale screen becomes a low-millions-scale one, putting ultralarge screening within reach of academic and small-biotech budgets.
insights.quote: an ATG prescreen involves docking 12 million molecules to explore the library of 69 billion compounds, which is >5,000-fold less computational effort than screening all molecules of the library
insights.locator: To investigate the effectiveness of the various parameters

insights.claim: Increasing prescreen thoroughness barely helps: one representative molecule per tranche at exhaustiveness 1 gave results similar to ten representatives or exhaustiveness 10, so the cheapest configuration is usually sufficient.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive, budget-relevant finding — spending more on prescreen depth is largely wasted, so the marginal compute belongs in the primary screen.
insights.quote: ATG prescreens with an exhaustiveness 1 and one representative molecule per tranche are expected to be sufficient for many applications
insights.locator: To investigate the effectiveness of the various parameters

insights.claim: An optional machine learning classifier trained on 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints from the prescreen, using the 75th percentile of docking scores as the decision boundary, further prioritizes molecules inside selected tranches.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The ML layer is deliberately simple and cheap — evidence that most of the gain comes from the property-binning structure rather than from model sophistication.

insights.claim: In benchmarks on ten protein targets, an adaptive screen of 100,000 molecules matched or beat a random screen of 1 million, a tenfold reduction in docking with no loss of docking performance.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A concrete efficiency ratio to benchmark competing screening platforms against; anything claiming less than 10x over random is not differentiated.
insights.quote: achieving a tenfold reduction in the number of compounds screened while maintaining similar docking performance

insights.claim: The benefit of adaptive prioritization is target dependent, with the largest gains on proteins whose pockets combine extensive hydrophobic surfaces with well-defined polar subpockets.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Efficiency claims should not be extrapolated across a portfolio — the method's payoff depends on pocket geometry, so per-target underwriting is required.
insights.quote: Proteins with complex, feature-rich binding pockets, particularly those combining extensive hydrophobic surfaces with well-defined polar subpockets, derived the greatest benefit from ATG-based prioritization and ML enhancement.
insights.locator: While ATG-based screens consistently outperformed random screening

insights.claim: The property-based binning strategy held up when the docking engine was swapped from QuickVina 2 to Smina with the Vinardo scoring function and to GWOVina with flexible side chains, showing the gains are not an artifact of one scoring function.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Robustness across scoring functions is what separates a real method from a tuned benchmark result — a diligence question to ask of every rival screening claim.
insights.quote: The physicochemical property-based binning remains effective independent of the docking protocol used.
insights.locator: To evaluate the sensitivity of our binning strategy

insights.claim: The prepared library covers 68.7 billion ready-to-dock molecules derived from 31.5 billion enumerated REAL Space compounds, expanded through stereoisomer and tautomer enumeration — roughly 45 times larger than the previous largest public ready-to-dock libraries, the 2018 REAL Database and ZINC20 at about 1.5 billion each.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A step-change in the free public screening asset; the moat that library preparation used to provide for well-funded groups largely disappears.
insights.quote: we prepared the 2022 version of the Enamine REAL Space into a ready-to-dock format, comprising 68.7 billion commercially available on-demand small molecules

insights.claim: The REAL Space compounds are built from 137,000 building blocks via 167 validated one-pot protocols with a reported 82% synthetic success rate across 386,000 experimental reactions run in 2021, and 99% obey Lipinski's Rule of Five.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: An 82% make rate is the number that converts virtual hits into orderable compounds; it is the key operational metric behind Enamine's on-demand business model.
insights.quote: This combinatorial framework enables high-throughput compound generation with a reported synthetic success rate of 82%, on the basis of 386,000 experimental reactions conducted in 2021.

insights.claim: Over 62 billion of the library's molecules (74%) contain at least one chiral center and 23 billion are halogenated including 17.4 billion fluorinated, the latter directly enabling 19F NMR binding assays without isotopically labeled protein.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A concrete assay-cost lever: fluorine-rich virtual hits let biophysics teams skip protein labeling, shortening the validation loop.
insights.quote: including 17.4 billion containing fluorine atoms, which are well suited for 19F nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)-based binding assays that do not require isotopically labeled proteins
insights.locator: The REAL Space is not only vast

insights.claim: The 18-dimensional property matrix has 24.4 billion theoretical tranches but only about 12 million are occupied, so the sparsity itself maps large unexplored regions of synthesizable chemical space.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Frames empty tranches as a synthesis roadmap — a defensible thesis for building-block and make-on-demand vendors targeting genuinely novel chemistry.
insights.quote: These unoccupied tranches present compelling opportunities for prospective synthesis campaigns to populate additional chemical spaces, enabling the development of molecules to selectively target previously undruggable regions of the proteome.

insights.claim: The platform demonstrated near-linear scaling to over 5.6 million AWS virtual CPUs, up from 160,000 vCPUs for the previous version, compressing billion-compound screens from weeks or months into hours.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A 35-fold jump in demonstrated parallelism; cloud burst capacity, not owned HPC, is now the reference infrastructure for drug-discovery screening.
insights.quote: we demonstrate near-linear scalability on AWS using over 5.6 million vCPUs, advancing parallelization in cloud-based drug discovery

insights.claim: Cost efficiency depends on architectural choices that tolerate preemption — roughly 30-minute subjobs with automatic reruns to exploit discounted AWS spot capacity, plus optional ARM CPU support.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Spot-and-ARM-native design is where the real dollar savings sit; a platform that cannot run on preemptible instances is structurally more expensive regardless of its algorithm.
insights.quote: ARM-based computing infrastructure can be more cost-efficient than traditional x86-based architectures.

insights.claim: The full ready-to-dock library occupies roughly 50 TB compressed per format and around 2 PB uncompressed, and is distributed through the AWS Open Data repository so users need no local storage.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Petabyte-scale data gravity means screening will happen where the library lives — a durable pull toward AWS for computational chemistry workloads.

insights.claim: The platform assembles over 1,500 docking protocols from more than 40 docking programs by combining sampling algorithms with scoring functions, including ML-based docking such as DiffDock, TANKBind and EquiBind, and supports RNA and DNA receptors as well as peptides.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Protocol breadth plus nucleic-acid receptor support extends virtual screening beyond protein targets, opening RNA-targeted small molecules to the same industrial-scale search.

insights.claim: The library is distributed in SELFIES format alongside SMILES and Parquet specifically to support generative models, because SELFIES guarantees syntactically valid molecules across arbitrary token sequences.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Makes the world's largest orderable library directly usable as generative-model training data — the bridge between de novo design and compounds you can actually buy.

insights.claim: Because each screening stage generates new labeled data, the active learning layer forms a closed loop that can be retrained on newly docked and experimentally assayed compounds for an arbitrary number of rounds.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The design that lets wet-lab assay results feed back into compute — the structural feature that separates a screening tool from a compounding data asset.
insights.quote: thereby forming a closed-loop active-learning cycle that progressively concentrates sampling on the most promising regions of chemical space
insights.locator: The AFLP module provides a pipeline

insights.claim: Deep-learning docking plus GPU acceleration is claimed to deliver a further 10 to 100-fold throughput increase on top of the up-to-1,000-fold saving from adaptive screening.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Stacked, these multipliers imply four to five orders of magnitude of cost reduction versus brute force, which resets what a hit-finding campaign should cost.
insights.quote: AdaptiveFlow incorporates deep-learning-based docking and GPU acceleration, achieving a further 10–100-fold increase in throughput

insights.claim: The team used ancestral sequence reconstruction to build a tetrapod ancestor of human FSP1 sharing 72.5% sequence identity that expressed at about 100 mg per litre in E. coli with a 62 °C melting temperature and full activity, solving the crystallography bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A reusable trick for structure-enabling difficult human proteins — worth watching as a standard tool for targets that resist crystallization.

insights.claim: Crystal structures showed that coenzyme Q and NAD(P)+ can bind FSP1 simultaneously in catalytically competent orientations, confirming a ternary complex mechanism and explaining why FSP1 also acts as a NAD(P)H oxidase.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Mechanistic clarity on a target that has attracted little chemical matter; enables rational design rather than trial-and-error screening for ferroptosis-sensitizing agents.
insights.quote: it is demonstrated that coenzyme Q and NAD(P)+ can simultaneously bind to the protein and this structural attribute perfectly aligns with the ternary complex mechanism evidenced by the kinetics data

insights.claim: Of 33 synthesized virtual hits, two showed at least 1.5 °C thermal shifts and over 50% inhibition at 10 µM, yielding Ki values of 0.283 µM for afi-FSP1-1 and 0.777 µM for afi-FSP1-2, comparable to or better than previously described FSP1 inhibitors.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A 2-in-33 hit rate reaching sub-micromolar on a poorly liganded target sets a realistic expectation for what an ultralarge adaptive screen returns.
insights.locator: Experimental validation: inhibitors extend from the coenzyme Q site to the NAD site

insights.claim: Cellular thermal shift assays in FSP1-expressing HEK293 cells showed 2.8 °C and 3.1 °C shifts, and afi-FSP1-1 combined with 0.5 µM erastin killed Jurkat leukemia cells at a potency matching the widely used iFSP1, with the effect fully rescued by liproxstatin-1.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Target engagement plus a rescuable, on-mechanism ferroptosis phenotype in cells — the evidence package needed before a ferroptosis-sensitizer program is credible.
insights.locator: Experimental validation: inhibitors extend from the coenzyme Q site to the NAD site

insights.claim: The best FSP1 inhibitors were 10 to 12-fold less effective against FSP1's NADH oxidase activity, and the authors propose this selectivity could convert the enzyme from antiferroptotic to actively proferroptotic — an untested but potentially high-value pharmacological concept.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: If validated, a mechanism that turns a cancer-resistance enzyme into a killing agent rather than merely disabling it — a differentiated positioning for FSP1 programs.
insights.quote: Inhibitors of this type may convert the enzyme from being antiferroptotic (coenzyme-Q-reducing activity) to being proferroptotic (uninhibited lipid-damaging ROS production).
insights.locator: Experimental validation: inhibitors extend from the coenzyme Q site to the NAD site

insights.claim: A second in-silico round seeded with the co-crystal structure of the first hit returned 20 analogs of which four were active, showing the platform supports structure-activity-relationship expansion and not just initial hit finding.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Closing the hit-to-lead loop computationally is where time and money actually get saved; hit discovery alone rarely changes a program's economics.
insights.locator: Experimental validation: inhibitors extend from the coenzyme Q site to the NAD site

themes.theme: PARP1 benchmark and the efficiency proof

insights.claim: Screening PARP1 produced seven inhibitors from 160 synthesized candidates, four with sub-250 nM IC50 values, and iParp1 hit 8.8 nM — comparable to FDA-approved olaparib, from a purely virtual screen with no prior knowledge of known inhibitors and no medicinal chemistry optimization.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Reaching approved-drug potency straight out of a virtual screen is the strongest available evidence that ultralarge screening can substitute for early medicinal chemistry.
insights.quote: iParp1 exhibited an IC50 of 8.8 nM, comparable to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug olaparib. This result is particularly notable given that our hits were derived from a purely virtual screen without any prior knowledge of known inhibitors

insights.claim: The most potent PARP1 hits showed reduced cellular activity in BRCA1-deficient triple-negative breast cancer clonogenic assays, attributed to poor membrane permeability caused by hydrolysis, exposing the standing gap between docking score and cell-level efficacy.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Docking does not model permeability or chemical stability — the honest caveat that keeps virtual-screening potency claims from translating directly into drug candidates.
insights.quote: although reduced cellular activity, especially for iParp1, was attributed to poor membrane permeability because of hydrolysis

insights.claim: The clearest efficiency proof is a head-to-head against the team's own prior work: earlier KEAP1–NRF2 nanomolar inhibitors required an unbiased screen of 1.3 billion molecules, while the adaptive FSP1 campaign achieved comparable success with 22 million docking instances.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A roughly 60-fold reduction in docking work for equivalent outcomes, measured against the same group's own baseline — the least gameable efficiency comparison in the paper.
insights.quote: while our previous identification of nanomolar KEAP1–NRF2 inhibitors8 required an unbiased screen of 1.3 billion molecules, the ATG-guided screen for FSP1 achieved comparable success with just 22 million docking instances

insights.claim: Adding new molecules to the library scales linearly and only representatives from newly populated tranches need to enter the prescreen set, so the prescreen cost does not grow with library size once the grid infrastructure exists.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Decoupling screening cost from library growth is the durable advantage here — it means trillion-compound libraries do not require trillion-scale compute budgets.
insights.quote: As new tranches beyond the 12 million currently populated are filled, only representatives from these newly populated tranches need to be incorporated into the prescreen set.
insights.locator: With the infrastructure now in place

insights.claim: The authors predict that maturing modalities such as molecular glues and targeted protein degraders will raise the value of being able to find small molecules that bind specific protein surfaces with functional consequences.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Positions ultralarge screening as infrastructure for the degrader wave rather than a competitor to it — relevant to how screening platforms should be valued.
insights.quote: As modalities like molecular glues and targeted protein degraders mature, the ability to identify small molecules that bind specific protein surfaces with functional consequences is becoming increasingly valuable.
insights.locator: With the infrastructure now in place
